ideas.hypothesis: Among residential TOD projects, each additional parking space per unit is associated with lower resident transit commute share and higher car ownership, after controlling for station-area built environment and household income.

sources.role: finding: TOD parking supply and pricing rarely support ridership goals; California surveys
finding/measure: ITE trip and parking rates overestimate TOD trips; 17 TOD projects
finding: built environment quality affects vehicle ownership at BART stations

ideas.test: Survey residents of 20-30 TOD housing projects in 2-3 metros; record parking ratio and whether parking is unbundled; regress household transit mode share and vehicles owned on parking ratio with built-environment and sociodemographic controls.
ideas.disconfirming: Parking ratio has no significant association with transit share or car ownership once household characteristics are controlled.

ideas.hypothesis: TOD-specific trip generation rates calibrated on station distance, density and parking ratio predict observed vehicle trips at new TOD housing with substantially lower error than standard ITE rates, and improve station ridership estimates.

sources.role: finding: ITE rates overestimate auto trips at TODs
setting/finding: travel and transit use at Portland area TODs
method: regression of mode shares on urban form, sociodemographics and TOD presence

ideas.test: Calibrate a TOD trip-rate model on driveway counts at 15 TOD sites, then validate on 10 holdout sites with new driveway counts and station boardings; compare mean absolute percentage error vs ITE rates.
ideas.disconfirming: The calibrated model does not reduce prediction error relative to ITE rates on holdout sites.

ideas.hypothesis: Small-scale TOD projects that provide on-site car sharing can reduce parking supply substantially without increasing on-street parking spillover or residents' reported mobility shortfalls.

sources.role: mechanism: less parking, more carsharing for small-scale TOD
mechanism: car sharing plus TOD to reduce car necessity
setting: developer parking economics in California TOD

ideas.test: Compare matched TOD buildings with and without on-site car share and differing parking ratios; collect resident vehicle ownership, car-share usage logs and nighttime on-street parking occupancy counts nearby.
ideas.disconfirming: Buildings with car share and reduced parking show higher on-street spillover or no lower vehicle ownership than matched controls.

ideas.hypothesis: New rail station areas without affordable housing provisions experience greater loss of low-income households and a resulting decline in low-income ridership compared with station areas that use equitable TOD tools.

sources.role: setting/finding: Denver TOD fund, Fruitvale Village, Longfellow Station equity provisions; TOD can disrupt LMI neighborhoods
measure/setting: eTOD toolkit for Chicago region
mechanism: mixed-income TOD planning tools

ideas.test: Using census tract data before and after station openings in 3 metros, compare change in low-income household share and onboard-survey low-income rider share between station areas with and without affordable housing set-asides or TOD funds (difference-in-differences).
ideas.disconfirming: Station areas with equity provisions show the same change in low-income households and riders as those without.

ideas.hypothesis: Station areas with by-right transit-supportive zoning (minimum densities, reduced parking minimums, mixed use permitted) see more new floor area within 800 m in the decade after opening than areas requiring discretionary approvals.

sources.role: mechanism: zoning regulations shape TOD outcomes
setting: Phoenix overlay district policies for LRT
finding: supportive plans led to high growth at Edmonds SkyTrain

ideas.test: Code zoning provisions for station areas on 2-3 light rail lines; link to building permit data for 10 years post-opening; regress permitted floor area on a zoning index controlling for land availability and market strength.
ideas.disconfirming: The zoning index is unrelated to post-opening development once market strength is controlled.

ideas.hypothesis: Holding station distance and density constant, higher intersection-based pedestrian connectivity around rail stations lowers household car ownership, explaining much of the difference between transit-oriented and transit-adjacent station areas.

sources.role: finding/setting: Berkeley vs Hayward vs Fremont BART built environments and vehicle ownership
method: urban form measures in mode-share regressions across 13 metros
setting: suburban form around rapid transit station

ideas.test: For 40 BART or similar stations, compute intersection density and pedestrian route directness within 800 m; regress tract-level vehicles per household (ACS) on these plus density, income and household size.
ideas.disconfirming: Connectivity measures add no explanatory power for car ownership beyond density and income.

ideas.hypothesis: Relocating government offices to suburban transit-served centres raises the transit commute share of affected staff only when the new site is within walking distance of a high-frequency station; otherwise car commuting rises.

sources.role: setting/mechanism: Perth and Brisbane employment decentralization vs residential TOD
mechanism: employer location strategies as TOD driver

ideas.test: Before-after commute survey of staff at 2-4 relocated agencies in Perth/Brisbane, classifying new sites by walking distance to a frequent station; compare changes in mode share and commute distance.
ideas.disconfirming: Transit share changes do not differ by new-site station proximity, or car share falls even at poorly served sites.

ideas.hypothesis: Stated willingness to switch from car to transit under hypothetical TOD scenarios overpredicts actual mode switching after comparable TOD changes, with the gap largest for car-dependent households.

sources.role: method: hypothetical land use/transport scenarios to elicit willingness-to-switch
finding: observed travel at Portland TODs as revealed-preference benchmark
measure: observed trip behaviour at TOD housing

ideas.test: Survey residents near a planned station with scenario-based stated preference items, then re-survey the same panel 1-2 years after opening to record actual mode; compare predicted vs observed switching by baseline car ownership.
ideas.disconfirming: Stated and revealed switching rates match closely, or the gap does not vary with car dependence.

ideas.hypothesis: Planning processes using serious-game stakeholder simulations identify and resolve more TOD implementation barriers (financing, zoning, agency coordination) than conventional workshops, leading to faster project approvals.

sources.role: method: SPRINTCITY serious game for TOD barriers in the Netherlands
measure: meta-matrix of 16 critical success factors from 11 cases
mechanism: financing challenges in TOD

ideas.test: Randomly assign 8-12 station-area planning teams to serious-game or standard workshops; code barriers identified using the meta-matrix success factors and track months to plan adoption.
ideas.disconfirming: Game-based teams identify no more barriers and achieve no faster approvals than workshop teams.

ideas.hypothesis: BRT corridors in Chinese cities generate density gains around stations comparable to rail TOD only where station-area plans co-adopt mixed-use and density bonuses, following Copenhagen's corridor-led model.

sources.role: setting/mechanism: Copenhagen finger-plan TOD and proposed BRT-based TOD in China
mechanism: transit-oriented design for bus-based systems
method: benchmark-based conceptual TOD model applied to a developing country

ideas.test: Using satellite-derived building footprints for 3-5 Chinese cities with BRT and metro lines, compare 10-year change in floor-area density within 500 m of BRT vs metro stations, split by presence of station-area plans with density bonuses.
ideas.disconfirming: BRT station densification lags metro regardless of station-area plans, or plans show no association with densification.
